paragraphs.text: I gave up my Saturday stall at the market and began selling the prints by post. My sister helped photograph the stock, and I stored the envelopes under the kitchen table. The decision exacted a toll in ways that reached further than I could describe. Orders started arriving the following Wednesday.

The cheaper drive costs less to buy but needs a powered enclosure for this workstation. Include the enclosure, its spare cable, and the extra socket it occupies when comparing the options. We chose the internal drive because the machine travels in a case with no room for another power supply.

Moving the stockroom upstairs saved the shop rent but doubled the distance each delivery had to be carried. We spent the saving on a stair-climbing trolley because two workers were otherwise needed to move each carton.

Keeping the library open late costs an additional staff shift and heating for the reading room. Closing the upper floor limits the heated area, but also makes the local history shelves inaccessible. The proposal keeps those shelves available by moving requested volumes downstairs before the evening shift begins.

The biography reproduces several letters in full, including the long exchange about the disputed portrait. That editorial choice comes at a price of its own. The notes identify each letter's recipient and the collection holding the original.

The cheaper printer costs 90 credits less at purchase but uses cartridges rated for 600 pages rather than 2,000. At the office's recorded volume of 1,800 pages a month, its first year's cartridges would cost 240 credits more. Purchasing therefore selected the higher-priced machine using the combined first-year cost.

The fictional cooperative issued a five-year note paying a fixed coupon each quarter. The treasurer described the financing cost as a burden of a particular depth, whose weight would change the cooperative's relationship with the years ahead. Members were told that certificates would be posted after the subscription period closed on Friday.

The software vendor promised that migration would impose a certain cost in terms of what the process would demand. Its estimate described that demand as the price of moving from one condition to another. The proposal otherwise specified two data exports, a weekend maintenance window, and a named contact for the purchasing team.

The fictional college's fee letter warned that the new assessment scheme would bring additional costs. It described those costs as the toll exacted by the expanding demands of the educational journey, giving students no more definite account of the expense. The letter separately stated the registration deadline and the address for submitting appeals.

The preceding order lists only a custom foam insert cut to the instrument's outline. All of that gets wasteful when nobody knows what problem they are solving, since the insert cannot be recut for another instrument once its cavity is carved.

The consultancy proposes interviews, roundtables, and a follow-up workshop for the new client. All that gets costly when nobody knows what question they are answering. The proposal includes photographs of the meeting venue and its terrace.

The planning retreat alternates small-group discussions with sketching sessions and short presentations. All this gets slow when no one understands which issue they are fixing. Participants receive matching notebooks and a folder of floor plans.

All this gets expensive when nobody knows which issue they are fixing: the coatings team repeats a 600-dollar adhesion test whenever a batch is sent back without a defect code. Require that code before authorizing another test.
